question: What is static pressure?

options.text: The pressure in a tube facing into the airflow
Ambient pressure plus dynamic pressure
The extra pressure caused by the aircraft's motion
The ambient pressure of the air the aircraft is in

explanation: Static pressure is the ambient pressure of the surrounding air, acting equally on all parts of an aircraft at rest in still air. The extra pressure from motion is dynamic pressure, and the two together are pitot (total) pressure.

question: Dynamic pressure depends on:

options.text: Air density only
True airspeed and air density
Static pressure and outside air temperature only
The aircraft's speed over the ground

explanation: Dynamic pressure is ½ρV², so it depends on air density and on true speed through the air. Ground speed plays no part.

question: What is pitot pressure made up of?

options.text: Static pressure plus dynamic pressure
Dynamic pressure minus static pressure
Static pressure minus dynamic pressure
Dynamic pressure only

explanation: The leading edges, and a tube facing into the airflow, feel total pressure: static plus dynamic. This total pressure is also called pitot pressure.

question: Why can dynamic pressure not be measured directly?

options.text: It is too small to move a capsule
It acts only on the trailing edges of the airframe
Static pressure is always present with it
It changes too quickly with altitude

explanation: Wherever dynamic pressure exists, static pressure is present too. Instruments therefore measure pitot pressure and static pressure and subtract one from the other: dynamic = pitot − static.

question: An instrument needs dynamic pressure. How does it obtain it?

options.text: It takes static pressure and subtracts it from a sealed reference
It adds static pressure to pitot pressure
It reads pitot pressure alone
It subtracts static pressure from pitot pressure

explanation: Dynamic = pitot − static. The airspeed indicator does this by feeding pitot pressure into a capsule and static pressure into the case around it.

question: Which of these instruments uses static pressure only?

options.text: The pitot-static probe heater
The Machmeter
The vertical speed indicator
The airspeed indicator

explanation: The altimeter and the vertical speed indicator need static pressure only. The airspeed indicator and the Machmeter need both pitot and static pressure.

question: Which pair of instruments needs both pitot and static pressure?

options.text: The airspeed indicator and the Machmeter
The altimeter and the vertical speed indicator
The airspeed indicator and the altimeter
The Machmeter and the vertical speed indicator

explanation: Both the airspeed indicator and the Machmeter work from dynamic pressure, so both need pitot and static. The altimeter and the VSI use static pressure alone.

question: Why must pitot and static pressures be sensed by devices outside the aircraft?

options.text: The air inside the cabin is too warm for the capsules
Inside pressure seldom matches outside
Pressure lines cannot be run inside a pressurised cabin
The instruments themselves are mounted outside

explanation: Cabin pressure and temperature seldom match the outside air, so both pressures are sensed by probes and vents on the outside of the aircraft and piped or transmitted to the instruments.

question: How is a pitot tube aligned?

options.text: Facing aft, away from the airflow
Parallel to the lateral axis
Parallel to the longitudinal axis, open end forward
At right angles to the airflow

explanation: The pitot tube is an open-ended tube parallel to the longitudinal axis, its open end facing into the airflow. The air is brought to rest in it, adding dynamic pressure to the static pressure already there.

question: To which instruments does the pitot tube connect?

options.text: The VSI and the Machmeter
The airspeed indicator and the Machmeter
The altimeter and the airspeed indicator
The altimeter and the VSI

explanation: The other end of the pitot tube leads to the airspeed capsules in the ASI and the Machmeter, the two instruments that need total pressure.

question: What is a static head?

options.text: A flat plate with a hole, fitted flush with the fuselage
A tube facing aft to avoid the dynamic pressure
An open-ended tube facing into the airflow
A tube sealed at the front, with side slots

explanation: A static head has its forward end sealed and holes or slots cut in the sides, so in theory it senses only static pressure. A flush plate with a hole is a static vent.

question: When the aircraft is moving, how does the pressure sensed by a static head compare with true static pressure?

options.text: It is slightly lower, because of suction
It is slightly higher, because of ram effect
It is exactly equal at all speeds
It is higher at low speed and lower at high speed

explanation: Air flowing past the side slots produces a slight suction, so the sensed static pressure is a little lower than true static. This is one part of position error.

question: In a combined pressure head, how are the pitot and static parts arranged?

options.text: They share a single line to the instruments
The pitot tube surrounds the static tube
The static tube surrounds the pitot tube
The two tubes are side by side, facing opposite ways

explanation: In a combined pitot-static pressure head the static tube surrounds the central pitot tube. Each has its own pressure line to the instruments.

question: Why is a pitot tube mounted on a strut or ahead of the nose?

options.text: So that it senses static pressure as well
To place it outside the boundary layer
To keep it away from the heater circuit
To avoid icing at low altitude

explanation: The boundary layer next to the skin is slowed by friction, so a pitot opening inside it would under-read. A strut on the fuselage side or a tube ahead of the nose places it in undisturbed air.

question: In which direction should the pitot opening face?

options.text: Parallel to the airflow in the normal flight attitude
Parallel to the airflow at the stall angle of attack
At right angles to the airflow in the normal flight attitude
Downwards, to let water drain out

explanation: The opening is designed to be parallel to the airflow in normal flight attitude so that the full dynamic pressure is recovered. At large angles of attack it is inclined to the flow and errors grow.

question: What is a stagnation wall in a pitot probe?

options.text: A heater element that keeps the probe free of ice
A drain that removes water from the probe
A baffle that separates pitot air from static air inside the head
A flat surface the air is stopped against

explanation: In some probes the air is brought to rest against a flat pressure-measuring surface, the stagnation wall, and the pressure is then passed up the pitot line. In simpler aircraft the pitot pressure is passed straight up the line.

question: Why is a pitot head heated?

options.text: To prevent insects entering on the ground
To correct the temperature error of the airspeed indicator
So that ice cannot block it
To warm the air before it reaches the capsule

explanation: Airspeed is critical to safety: too slow and the aircraft stalls, too fast and it is overstressed. An electric anti-icing heater coil therefore keeps the probe clear; errors caused by the heating are reduced by design and calibration.

question: Why does a pitot head have drain holes?

options.text: To let static pressure into the pitot line
To drain water so that ice cannot form in it
To cool the heater element
To reduce the dynamic pressure at high speed

explanation: If water is drained it cannot freeze in the probe. The drain holes cause a small loss of pressure, which is allowed for in design and calibration.

question: What is the effect of a pitot probe's drain holes on the pressure it senses?

options.text: A small loss, allowed for in the calibration
A rise in pressure at high speed
None, because they are closed in flight
A large loss that makes the ASI unusable in rain

explanation: The drain holes leak a little pressure, but the loss is known and is built into the design and calibration of the system.

question: How should the opening of a static source be aligned?

options.text: Parallel to the airflow, facing forward
Parallel to the airflow, facing aft
At 45° to the airflow
At right angles to the airflow

explanation: An opening at right angles to the airflow senses static pressure with no component of dynamic pressure. A forward-facing opening would sense pitot pressure.

question: What is position error (also called pressure error)?

options.text: Error caused by reading the instrument from the side
Error due to the sources sensing disturbed air
Error caused by the pilot's seat position
Error from friction and lag inside the instrument's own mechanism

explanation: Position error arises because the airflow around the probe or vent, affected by speed, attitude and turbulence, makes the sensed pressure differ from the true pressure. It is a property of where the source is placed.

question: How does position error change as airspeed increases?

options.text: It disappears
It changes sign at the stall speed
It becomes smaller
It generally becomes greater

explanation: As speed rises the suction effect and the turbulence around the probes increase, so position error grows. Large angles of attack at low speed also increase it.

question: Why is position error often large at large angles of attack?

options.text: The head is inclined to the airflow
The heater cannot keep up with the airflow
The static vent is in the boundary layer
The dynamic pressure is too high

explanation: At high angles of attack, usually at low speed, the probe meets the airflow at an angle, so the pressure it senses is in error. This is why position error is often listed for each flap setting.

question: Why may a flight manual list different position error corrections for each flap setting?

options.text: Flap reduces the dynamic pressure to a constant
Flap switches the instruments to the alternate static source
Flap changes the attitude and the airflow around the sources
Flap changes the static pressure at the vents to zero

explanation: Lowering flap alters the angle of attack and the flow around the probes and vents, so the position error is different for each configuration.

question: Position error depends mainly on:

options.text: Head position, airspeed and attitude
Outside air temperature, humidity and altitude
Instrument friction and pointer balance
Altitude and the altimeter subscale setting

explanation: The three main factors are where the pressure head is fitted, the airspeed and the attitude (angle of attack). Temperature and friction cause other errors.

question: Turbulence produced by a pressure head mainly affects which pressure?

options.text: Neither, because it is downstream of both
The pitot pressure
The static pressure
Both equally

explanation: The turbulence created by the head itself forms downstream of the pitot opening, where the static slots are, so it distorts the static reading rather than the pitot reading.

question: Why were static vents introduced in place of static heads?

options.text: Static heads cannot be heated
Static vents measure dynamic pressure as well
The head's own turbulence spoils its pitot reading at high speed
The head's own turbulence spoils its static reading

explanation: Because the head's own turbulence affects the static slots most, static pressure was taken instead from a vent on the fuselage, with pitot pressure taken from a simple pitot head.

question: What is a static vent?

options.text: A scoop facing into the airflow
A small hole in a flush plate
A tube with a sealed nose and slots in its sides
A tube facing forward on a strut

explanation: A static vent is a small circular hole in a flat metal plate, at a place on the fuselage where true or nearly true static pressure is found over the whole speed range.

question: Why is a static vent fitted on each side of the fuselage and the two interconnected?

options.text: To separate the captain's and first officer's pitot pressure
To double the pressure sent to the instruments
To largely cancel errors caused by yawing
To provide a spare in case one is blocked by ice

explanation: In a yaw or sideslip one vent senses a higher pressure and the other a lower one. Connecting them averages the two, so the error largely cancels; this is called cross-balancing.

question: Which is an advantage of a static vent over a static head?

options.text: It measures both pitot and static pressure
It needs no heating in any flight conditions at all
It cannot be blocked by ice or insects
Smoother airflow, so a more accurate reading

explanation: The vent sits in smoother airflow, so the static pressure is more accurate, and errors from sideslip and yaw are reduced. Vents can still be blocked, which is why alternate sources and covers exist.

question: What is cross-balancing of static vents?

options.text: Using a cabin source to balance a blocked vent
Linking vents on both sides to reduce yaw error
Feeding the standby altimeter from the main vents
Comparing the captain's and the first officer's static pressures

explanation: Duplicate vents either side of the fuselage, connected together, average out the pressure differences caused by sideslip or yaw.

question: Why may a high-speed aircraft use a combined pitot-static probe instead of static vents?

options.text: Shock waves cause large errors at a vent
Static vents cannot be heated at high altitude
A probe has no position error at any Mach number
A probe also measures total air temperature

explanation: At high Mach numbers shock waves can spoil the pressure at a fuselage vent. A carefully designed probe keeps position error within acceptable limits.

question: Which is a typical location for a high-speed pitot-static probe?

options.text: Inside the engine intake
Ahead of a wing tip
On top of the cockpit roof
On the trailing edge of the flap

explanation: Typical locations are ahead of a wing tip, under a wing, ahead of the fin tip, at the side of the nose and ahead of the nose. The choice depends on the aircraft's aerodynamics.

question: What decides where a pitot-static probe or vent is placed?

options.text: The position of the instrument panel
The length of the pressure lines
The location of the electrical bus
The aerodynamics of the aircraft

explanation: The site is chosen where the airflow gives the smallest and most consistent pressure error over the speed range, which depends on the aircraft's aerodynamic shape.

question: What causes manoeuvre-induced error?

options.text: A wrong subscale setting
Viewing the instrument from the side
Brief pressure changes at the vents, and line delays
Friction in the capsule linkage and the gearing of the pointer

explanation: Manoeuvre-induced error comes from brief fluctuations of pressure at the static vents and from the time pressure changes take to travel up the lines to the instruments.

question: Do servo altimeters and air data computers suffer from manoeuvre-induced error?

options.text: Yes, because they use the same static vents
Only when the alternate static source is in use
No, because they are electrically driven
No, because they correct for it automatically

explanation: Servo altimeters and air data computers take their static pressure from the same vents as simple instruments, so they share the manoeuvre-induced error.

question: What are the main causes of the airflow changes that produce manoeuvre-induced error?

options.text: Electrical interference from the pitot heater circuits
Changes in engine power at constant attitude
Angle of attack changes, and flap or gear movement
Changes in outside air temperature

explanation: Changing the angle of attack, and the turbulence from lowering or raising flaps and landing gear, alter the flow over the static vents and produce the error.

question: How does manoeuvre-induced error most commonly appear?

options.text: As a total loss of the reading
As a marked lag
As a fixed offset that never changes with speed
As a reading that oscillates at constant speed

explanation: The most common sign is a marked lag: the pressure instruments are slow to show the change that has happened.

question: When are manoeuvre-induced errors usually worst?

options.text: When pitch attitude changes
In straight and level cruise
During a steady roll at a constant pitch attitude
In a steady turn at constant height

explanation: The errors are larger for changes of pitch than for yaw or roll, so they are worst when a climb or descent begins and when the aircraft levels out.

question: Which phases of flight are particularly vulnerable to manoeuvre-induced error?

options.text: Cruise at constant Mach number
Taxiing and holding on the ground
A steady, constant-rate descent on the glide path
A go-around, and rough air

explanation: A go-around combines a pitch change with flap and gear movement, and rough air brings continual pressure changes; both make the error worst.

question: Manoeuvre-induced errors are:

options.text: Constant at a given altitude
Predictable and listed in the flight manual
Always in the sense of over-reading
Unpredictable in both size and sense

explanation: Because they cannot be predicted in size or direction, pressure instruments cannot be trusted for accurate instantaneous values or rates during manoeuvres.

question: Which instruments should be the primary reference during in-flight manoeuvres?

options.text: The standby altimeter
The vertical speed indicator
The gyroscopic instruments
The pressure instruments

explanation: Pressure instruments, the VSI above all, are unreliable during manoeuvres because of manoeuvre-induced error. Gyroscopic instruments such as the attitude indicator are the primary reference.

question: How long can manoeuvre-induced error persist at 30 000 ft after the controls have stopped moving?

options.text: About 30 seconds
About 10 seconds
About 1 second
About 3 seconds

explanation: Typical values are about three seconds at low altitude, increasing to about ten seconds at 30 000 ft, and longer still for VSIs.

question: At low altitude, how long might manoeuvre-induced error persist after the control surfaces have stopped moving?

options.text: About 3 seconds
Less than a tenth of a second
About 10 seconds
About 30 seconds

explanation: About three seconds at low altitude is typical, rising to about ten seconds at 30 000 ft because the thinner air takes longer to settle the pressure in the lines.

question: Which pressure instrument suffers longest from manoeuvre-induced lag?

options.text: The Machmeter
The vertical speed indicator
The altimeter
The airspeed indicator

explanation: The VSI works on a rate of change of static pressure through a restricted choke, so manoeuvre-induced errors last longer in it than in the other pressure instruments.

question: In modern aircraft, how is pitot and static information usually carried from the sources?

options.text: By long pressure pipelines to every instrument
By mechanical push-rods
By fibre optic light guides only
Electrically, by wires or digital data buses

explanation: Older and simple systems use pipelines; modern aircraft often have pressure transducers at the sources and carry the data electrically, often in digital form on data buses.

question: Why do pitot and static pipelines have water traps?

options.text: To collect water before it can block the lines
To damp out rapid pressure changes
To warm the air before it reaches the instruments
To separate pitot air from static air in a combined line

explanation: Water in the lines can block them or freeze. Both pitot and static pipelines therefore have built-in water traps.

question: What does an analogue/digital interface unit do in a modern pitot-static system?

options.text: Converts digital data back into a pressure
Heats the pressure transducers
Digitises the pressure measurement
Mixes the pitot and static pressures

explanation: The pressure measurement itself is analogue; A/D interface units turn it into digital data, usually for the air data computer.

question: In a large aircraft, where is the digitised pitot and static data usually sent?

options.text: To the air data computer
To the inertial reference system
Directly to the flight data recorder only
To the cabin pressure controller

explanation: In modern aircraft the digital pressure data usually goes to the air data computer, which works out airspeed, altitude, vertical speed and Mach number for the displays and other systems.

question: Are the pitot systems of a large aircraft normally cross-coupled?

options.text: Only when a pitot heater fails
Yes, but only for the standby instruments
Yes; both pitot sources are mixed for every instrument
No; each pitot source feeds its own side's instruments

explanation: The left pitot feeds the left instruments and the right pitot the right. The systems may be compared, with a warning for a difference of, say, 5 kt, but pitot pressure is not cross-fed.

question: A flight instrument system compares the two airspeed channels. What happens if they disagree by more than about 5 kt?

options.text: The pitot systems are automatically cross-connected
The standby ASI is switched in automatically
A warning is given; pitot pressure is not cross-fed
The lower reading is replaced by the higher one

explanation: Modern systems may monitor the two outputs and warn of a discrepancy above a set value such as 5 kt. They do not mix or cross-feed pitot pressure.

question: How is each static system of a large aircraft normally arranged?

options.text: Both systems share a single vent on the belly
From its own vents on both sides, mixed
It uses the cabin pressure as its source
From one vent on its own side of the fuselage only

explanation: Static systems are almost always cross-coupled: each has its own left and right vents, mixed together, to reduce errors from yaw and sideslip.

question: Which instruments does the standby static system of a large aircraft usually serve?

options.text: All the captain's pressure instruments
The standby VSI and the standby Machmeter
The standby ASI and the standby altimeter
The air data computers

explanation: Large aircraft have a standby pair of static vents for the standby airspeed indicator and altimeter. A standby VSI or Machmeter is not normally fitted.

question: The right static vent is blocked and the aircraft yaws to the right. How will the altimeter read?

options.text: It under-reads
It returns to zero
It over-reads
It reads correctly

explanation: With the right vent blocked, only the left vent supplies the system. Yawing right swings the left side of the fuselage into the airflow, so the left vent senses a higher pressure, and a higher static pressure makes the altimeter under-read.

question: An aircraft is sideslipping to the right with the left static vent blocked. The altimeter will:

options.text: Freeze at the altitude of the blockage
Read correctly, because the vents are cross-connected
Over-read
Under-read

explanation: In a sideslip to the right the relative airflow comes from the right, so the right vent, the only one working, faces it and senses a raised pressure. Higher static pressure means a lower indicated altitude.

question: What is the purpose of an alternate static source in a light aircraft?

options.text: To pressurise the cabin
To replace blocked static vents
To test the instruments before flight
To supply pitot pressure if the pitot tube becomes blocked with ice

explanation: If the static head or vents are blocked, the pilot can select an alternate static source with a selector in the cabin.

question: In which aircraft may the alternate static source be taken from inside the cabin?

options.text: Only aircraft with an air data computer
Pressurised aircraft only
Any aircraft, if the cabin is vented
Unpressurised aircraft only

explanation: Cabin pressure in a pressurised aircraft is far above outside static pressure, so a cabin source is only usable in an unpressurised aircraft.

question: When the alternate static source is selected, the pressure sensed is usually:

options.text: Lower than ambient
Exactly ambient, because the cabin is vented to outside
Equal to the pitot pressure
Higher than ambient, because of ram air

explanation: Whether the alternate source is outside or in an unpressurised cabin, suction usually makes it read lower than ambient. Lower static pressure makes the altimeter and ASI over-read.

question: Why is the alternate static source less accurate than the normal static vents?

options.text: The alternate source is not connected to the altimeter
The normal vents are in the best position
The alternate source has no water trap or drain
The alternate source feeds pitot pressure as well

explanation: The primary vents are placed where the pressure error is smallest. The alternate source is wherever it can be fitted, so its error is larger.

question: Where are the instrument corrections for use of the alternate static source found?

options.text: On a placard on each pitot head
In the aerodrome's published charts
In the aircraft's operating data manual
They are applied automatically by the instruments

explanation: The instruments are calibrated for the error at their normal source. When the alternate source is used, the correction values are given in the aircraft's operating data or flight manual.

subtopic: Pitot covers and static vent plugs
question: Why are pitot and static openings covered when the aircraft is parked?

options.text: To keep the instruments warm overnight
Dirt or insects could block them
To stop the static pressure leaking out of the lines
To keep the heater from switching on

explanation: The openings are very sensitive to contamination. They also tend to stay warmer than the rest of the aircraft at night, which attracts insects. Covers and plugs keep them clean.

subtopic: Pitot covers and static vent plugs
question: Why do insects often settle in pitot and static openings at night?

options.text: The heaters stay on after shutdown
The openings are lit up by the navigation lights at night
They stay warmer than the airframe
The openings contain water from the drains

explanation: Pitot and static openings tend to be warmer at night than the rest of the airframe, making them attractive resting places for insects.

subtopic: Pitot covers and static vent plugs
question: Why do pitot covers and static plugs carry a long streamer?

options.text: To stop them blowing away in wind
To earth any static charge from the airframe
To show the wind direction on the ramp
So that they are not overlooked

explanation: A conspicuous streamer, up to about a metre long, makes sure the covers and plugs are seen and removed during the external checks.

question: How can a pitot heater be checked before flight?

options.text: Switch on briefly and feel the probe for warmth
Switch it on and leave it on until the engines have been started
Check that the static vent is warm
Blow into the probe and watch the ASI

explanation: Switch the heater on briefly, about 30 seconds, and carefully feel the probe. Then switch it off again so that it does not burn out on the ground.

question: Apart from feeling the probe, which other check may show that a pitot heater is working?

options.text: An ammeter rise or a compass deflection
A rise in the ASI reading on the ground
A fall in the altimeter reading
A green light beside the airspeed indicator dial

explanation: Switching on the heater draws current, so the ammeter rises, and on some aircraft the current deflects the magnetic compass.

question: Why should the pitot cover be removed before the heater is checked?

options.text: The heater will not work with the cover on
The cover stops the current flowing
The heater can burn or melt the cover
The cover makes the ASI read high

explanation: The heated probe can burn or melt a canvas or rubber cover. Covers and plugs should be removed before the heaters are tested.

question: Why is the pitot heater switched off again after the ground test?

options.text: To save fuel during taxi
Because it interferes with the radios on the ground
Because it would melt the static plug
To stop it burning out without cooling airflow

explanation: On the ground there is no airflow to carry the heat away, so the heater could overheat and burn out. It is switched on again in the pre-take-off checks.

question: When are pitot heaters normally switched on and off?

options.text: On in the descent and off after landing
On before take-off, off after landing
On at engine start and off again at engine shutdown
Only when visible icing is encountered

explanation: Heaters are normally switched on as part of the pre-take-off checks and off as part of the after-landing checks. Modern systems warn if the heaters are off in flight.

question: On a combined pitot-static probe, does the static opening receive heat?

options.text: Only above 20 000 ft
Yes, it is heated as a consequence of the pitot heater
Only when the alternate static is selected
No, static openings are never heated

explanation: All aircraft have pitot heaters, and on a combined probe the static opening is heated as a consequence. Some static sensors also have heating of their own.

question: Which item is part of the preflight check of the pitot-static system?

options.text: All covers and plugs removed and stowed
The altimeter set to 1013 hPa
The alternate static source selected
The pitot heater left on until take-off

explanation: The checks are: all covers and plugs removed and stowed, all tubes, holes and slots clear, and the pitot heater working.
